glossary.Renal function: How well the kidneys are filtering the blood, usually judged by creatinine and eGFR.
glossary.Precipitants: Things that trigger or tip a patient into a condition.
glossary.Sepsis: Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by the body's response to infection.
glossary.CKD: Chronic kidney disease: kidney damage or reduced function lasting over 3 months.
glossary.MRI: Magnetic resonance imaging, a scan using magnets; some contrast agents for it can harm kidneys.
glossary.Contrast agents: Dyes given for scans to make structures stand out; some are toxic to the kidneys.
glossary.Non-specific: Symptoms that could be due to many different conditions.
glossary.Non-oliguric: AKI where urine output stays normal despite falling kidney function.
glossary.Fluid overload: Too much fluid in the body, causing swelling, breathlessness and crackles in the lungs.
glossary.Perfusion: Blood flow delivering oxygen to a tissue or organ.
glossary.Hypovolaemic shock: Dangerously low blood pressure and poor perfusion from loss of blood or fluid volume.
glossary.Mucous membranes: The moist linings of the mouth, nose and eyes; dry ones suggest dehydration.
glossary.Uraemic tinge: A brown-grey or sallow skin colour from retained waste products in kidney failure.
glossary.Tachycardia: Heart rate above 100 beats per minute.
glossary.Urinary sodium: The concentration of sodium in the urine; low when the kidney is holding on to salt.
glossary.Stones: Hard crystal deposits in the urinary tract that can block urine flow.
glossary.Acute urinary retention: Sudden painful inability to pass urine despite a full bladder.
glossary.Suprapubic: The area just above the pubic bone, where the bladder sits.
glossary.Palpable bladder: A full, distended bladder that can be felt as a mass above the pubic bone.
glossary.Creatine kinase: An enzyme released from damaged muscle; very high levels suggest rhabdomyolysis.
glossary.Oedema: Swelling from fluid collecting in the tissues.
glossary.Crackles: Fine crackling lung sounds on listening, often from fluid in the alveoli.
glossary.U&Es: Urea and electrolytes: blood test for sodium, potassium, urea and creatinine.
glossary.Blood gas: Test of blood pH, oxygen, CO2, bicarbonate and often potassium and lactate.
glossary.Urine dipstick: A test strip dipped in urine to detect blood, protein, glucose, leucocytes and nitrites.
glossary.Glomerular: To do with the glomeruli, the filtering units of the kidney.
glossary.Protein electrophoresis: A blood test separating proteins to look for a paraprotein, as in myeloma.
glossary.C3: A complement protein; low levels suggest immune-complex kidney disease.
glossary.C4: A complement protein; low with C3 in conditions such as lupus nephritis.
glossary.ANA: Antinuclear antibodies, a screening test for autoimmune disease such as lupus.
glossary.dsDNA: Anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies, specific for systemic lupus erythematosus.
glossary.Immunoglobulins: Antibodies; measured to look for myeloma or immune disorders.
glossary.Diuretics: Drugs that increase urine output, such as furosemide.
glossary.Digoxin: A heart drug for AF and heart failure that can build up to toxic levels in AKI.
glossary.Metformin: A diabetes drug that can cause lactic acidosis when kidney function falls.
glossary.Methotrexate: An immunosuppressant and chemotherapy drug cleared by the kidneys, toxic if it accumulates.
glossary.Cardioprotective aspirin: Low-dose aspirin taken to prevent heart attacks and strokes.
glossary.Lithium: A mood stabiliser for bipolar disorder, cleared by the kidneys, with a narrow safe range.
glossary.0.9% saline: Normal saline, a standard IV fluid of salt in water.
glossary.Catheterisation: Passing a tube into the bladder to drain urine.
glossary.Vascular catheter: A tube placed into a large vein, for example for dialysis.
glossary.Cardiac membrane: The membrane of heart muscle cells, made unstable by high potassium.
glossary.Contraindications: Reasons a treatment should not be given.
glossary.Dialysis: Artificially removing waste, potassium, acid and fluid from the blood when the kidneys cannot.
glossary.Intoxication: Poisoning by a substance, such as lithium or salicylate, that dialysis can remove.
glossary.Pericarditis: Inflammation of the sac around the heart, causing chest pain eased by sitting forward.
glossary.Encephalopathy: Brain dysfunction causing confusion or drowsiness, here from toxins in kidney failure.
glossary.Pulmonary oedema: Fluid in the lung air spaces, causing breathlessness.
glossary.Bibasal crackles: Crackles heard at the bottom of both lungs.
glossary.Renal blood flow: The blood supply reaching the kidneys.
glossary.Osmolality: The concentration of dissolved particles in a fluid; high means concentrated urine.
glossary.Tubular flow: The rate of fluid moving through the kidney tubules.
glossary.Tubular epithelial cells: The cells lining the kidney tubules that reabsorb salt and water.
glossary.Ischaemia: Lack of blood supply to a tissue.
glossary.Fractional excretion of sodium: The percentage of filtered sodium that ends up in urine.
glossary.Intratubular pressure: Pressure inside the kidney tubules, which rises when urine flow is blocked.
glossary.Filtration gradient: The pressure difference that drives fluid out of the glomerular capillaries into the tubule.
glossary.Nephrostomy: A tube inserted through the skin into the kidney to drain urine above a blockage.
glossary.Efferent arteriolar tone: How constricted the vessel leaving the glomerulus is; constriction keeps filtration pressure up.
glossary.Hypoperfusion: Reduced blood flow to an organ.
glossary.Membrane depolarisation: The cell membrane becoming less negative, making heart cells unstable.
glossary.Myocytes: Muscle cells; cardiac myocytes are heart muscle cells.
glossary.Bicarbonate: The main alkali buffer in blood, made by the kidneys to neutralise acid.
